passage: In the school design lab, Lavanya looked at the tasks on the board for the model bridge: paint, wire the lights, test, build the frame. Vijay was ready to paint. "Not yet," said Lavanya. "Paint needs a dry frame, and the test can't happen until the wiring is done. Those two start the chain." She drew arrows: frame, then dry, then paint; circuit, then test. "Frame glue first, today, because it needs a whole day to dry. Circuit tomorrow. Meanwhile, Vijay, you can do the signboard and the poster. Nothing waits on those." Vijay shrugged, then began cutting card, his tongue between his teeth. By Friday the frame was dry and painted, and the little lights blinked on the first try.

qa.q: Why could Vijay not start painting at once?
qa.a: Painting needs a dry frame, and the frame glue needed a whole day to dry.

qa.q: How does Vijay feel when told not to paint yet?
qa.a: Vijay is a little reluctant and shrugs, but settles into the signboard work with concentration.

qa.q: What could Lavanya do if the glue takes longer than a day to dry, and why?
qa.a: Lavanya could move other tasks such as the poster and the wiring ahead while waiting, because independent jobs can run in parallel.

qa.q: How might Lavanya see Vijay being ready to paint?
qa.a: Lavanya sees the painting as coming too early, since paint needs a dry frame, so she gives Vijay the signboard and poster, which nothing waits on.

grounding: The leader sees that painting cannot start until the frame dries and testing needs a working circuit, so she starts those tasks first and lets independent ones run in parallel.
